title: THE HIRELING
mv: But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
mvp: “But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.” John 10:12
assignment: Mention five (5) consequences of being a hireling (2X5=10 marks).

b.x: Jesus describes a hireling as someone who looks like a shepherd, acts like one, but runs away when danger comes (John 10:12). Sadly, the spirit of the hireling is still alive today. Have you ever worked with someone who only shows up anywhere there is gain but never cares about the people or the purpose of the job? This lesson challenges us to examine our motives in service: a true shepherd or a hireling in disguise?

i: Serves for personal gain. The hireling’s motivation is wages, recognition or benefits. He does not care to know the sheep or understand their needs (John 10:12-13).

Lacks commitment and loyalty. Works only when it is convenient or profitable. The hireling’s service is transactional; no reward, no service. When challenges arise, he abandons his responsibility (Malachi 1:10; John 10:12).
Seeks position and reward rather than responsibility. He desires titles or offices for personal comfort rather than to serve God’s purpose (1 Samuel 2:36).
Fails in times of test or persecution. They cannot endure hardship for Christ’s sake; they quit when the cost is high (Matthew 13:20-21; Zechariah 11:17).
Seeks human approval rather than God’s commendation. A hireling adjusts his message or actions to please people, not God (Galatians 1:10).

b.x: In John 10:11-13, Jesus contrasts Himself, being the Good Shepherd, with the hireling who “sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep, and flees.” The hireling’s motive is not love but gain; his service is driven by wages, not by compassion. The difference between the hireling and the Good Shepherd is not in their position but in their heart and motive (1 Peter 5:2-4). Both may hold the title of “shepherd,” but only one truly loves the sheep.

The hireling works for what he can get; the Good Shepherd serves for what He can give, even His life. Jesus calls us not just to serve in His vineyard, but to serve with ‘‘His heart ’’ - one that stays even when it costs, one that loves even when it hurts (2 Timothy 2:3-4). The hireling neglects or exploits the weak, seeks independence and avoids correction (Ezekiel 34:2-4) while the Good Shepherd heals, restores, and strengthens the weak, submits to correction and is accountable (1 Corinthians 9:16-17; John 6:38). The result is that the hireling’s flock are scattered and destroyed while the Good Shepherd’s flock are preserved, united, and multiplied (John 10:28-29). True ministry is not about reward, fame, or recognition; it is about faithfulness. God is still seeking men and women who will stand in the gap, not for gain, but out of genuine love for His flock.
Some serve when it is convenient, give to be noticed, and withdraw when sacrifice is required, but God is looking for true shepherds.

i: Mention five characteristics of a hireling.
Differentiate between a hireling and a good Shepherd.
